I recently completed three of the top Christian financial education programs for churches: SeedTime’s True Financial Freedom, Dave Ramsey’s Financial Peace University, and Crown Financial’s MoneyLife.

These popular programs all claim to help you get control of your finances from a biblical perspective. However, they go about it in different ways with varying teaching styles and philosophies.

In this post, I’ll provide an in-depth look at each program – breaking down the unique features, strengths, weaknesses, and what’s actually included when you buy in.

According to recent reports, my goal is to give you the real deal on these courses so you can determine which one (if any) is the best fit for transforming your financial life in a way that aligns with your faith. Whether you’re deep in debt, building wealth, or simply trying to honor God with your money, this comparison will help guide your journey.

Let’s dive into the nitty-gritty details of each program:.

It has been revealed that when it comes to pricing, Financial Peace University from Dave Ramsey sits in the middle. For an individual membership, it’s $69.99. They also offer bulk pricing for churches starting at around $800 for 10 memberships.

It has been revealed that on the higher end, Seedtime’s True Financial Freedom charges $149 for an individual/couple license with regular deals making it available as low as $74. But they have some solid deals for Churches – you can get a bulk student license for as low as $48 per person if you buy multiple licenses. Or there’s an annual church subscription starting as low as $750 per year based on average attendance.

The most affordable option is Crown Financial’s MoneyLife course at just $29.95 for an individual purchase. I couldn’t find any publicly listed bulk pricing for churches, but being a non-profit, I’d expect them to be the cheapest route for congregations.

But as you’ll see, there are plenty more differences beyond just the price tags when comparing what’s actually included in each program.

According to recent reports, true Financial Freedom, created by Bob Lotich and his wife Linda from SeedTime, is a financial literacy video course designed for churches that strikes a beautiful balance between biblical wisdom and practical money management strategies. The program’s goal is to equip Christians with the tools and mindset they need to experience true financial freedom while making an eternal impact for God’s Kingdom.

One of the standout features of True Financial Freedom is the engaging and relatable teaching style of Bob and Linda. They share their own financial struggles and triumphs with humor, transparency, and grace, making participants feel like they’re learning from wise, caring friends rather than aloof experts. This approach creates a safe, non-judgmental environment where participants can openly discuss their financial challenges and celebrate their progress.

The program offers several unique benefits, such as the “Never 100” rule (their ‘done-is-better-than-perfect’ approach to adjust spending) and the “Straight A” strategy for automating finances. These concepts are not only memorable but also highly actionable in helping participants take control of their money and build lasting wealth.

Industry observers note that another strength of True Financial Freedom is its emphasis on creating a personalized financial strategy. Through interactive workshops, participants are guided in developing a custom blueprint that fits their unique situation, goals, and values. This approach recognizes that there’s no one-size-fits-all solution to personal finance and empowers participants to take ownership of their financial journey.

Recent findings suggest that true Financial Freedom is perfect for Christians who want to learn how to thrive financially while staying grounded in the Bible. The program teaches participants how to avoid the extremes of being “so heavenly-minded they’re no earthly good” or becoming so focused on building worldly wealth that they lose sight of what truly matters.

With its grace-filled approach and practical tools, True Financial Freedom helps Christians find the balance needed to change their financial life and make a lasting difference in the world in the process.

Financial Peace University, created by Dave Ramsey and his team at Ramsey Solutions, is a highly popular financial education program that has helped countless individuals and families get out of debt and build wealth. The program’s primary goal is to guide participants through a proven, step-by-step approach to taking control of their money and achieving financial peace.

In a recent development, dave Ramsey, the face of Financial Peace University, is known for his high-energy, tough love teaching style. He delivers hard-hitting truths about money with a sense of urgency and conviction that inspires participants to take action. However, some may find his approach a bit intense or even abrasive at times, likening it to going through bootcamp. While this style resonates with some, it may not be everyone’s preferred learning environment.

It has been revealed that the cornerstone of Financial Peace University is the “Baby Steps” system, a clear, prescriptive initiative for getting out of debt and building wealth. The program heavily emphasizes the debt snowball method, which involves paying off debts from smallest to largest, regardless of interest rates. This approach has proven highly effective in keeping participants motivated and helping them experience quick wins on their debt-free journey.

According to recent reports, while Financial Peace University does incorporate some biblical principles, its overall approach is more secular in nature. The program focuses primarily on the practical nuts and bolts of money management, with less emphasis on exploring the deeper spiritual implications of financial stewardship.

In a recent development, financial Peace University is best suited for individuals and families who are drowning in debt and need a clear, actionable strategy to get back on track. The program’s structured approach and intense motivation can be a lifeline for those feeling overwhelmed by their financial situation. However, those seeking a more personalized, grace-filled approach that deeply integrates biblical wisdom may find other programs more appealing.

MoneyLife, offered by Crown Financial, is a financial education program that takes a deeply biblical approach to money management. The program’s primary goal is to guide Christians in understanding and applying God’s financial principles to their lives, emphasizing the importance of seeing God as the ultimate provider and owner of all resources.

One of MoneyLife’s distinguishing features is its strong focus on biblical teachings and spiritual practices related to money. The program dives deep into exploring how our financial decisions can reflect our faith and values, encouraging participants to align their money management with biblical principles. This emphasis on the spiritual aspects of finance sets MoneyLife apart from other programs that may focus more heavily on practical strategies.

The teaching style in MoneyLife tends to be more academic and classroom-like compared to other programs. Participants can expect a significant amount of reading materials and written assessments throughout the course. While this approach may appeal to those who prefer a studious learning environment, it may not be as engaging for individuals who thrive on interactive, video-based content.

MoneyLife offers some unique elements, such as personality assessments that help participants understand how their natural tendencies impact their financial decisions. The program also includes exercises like the transfer of ownership, which guides participants in acknowledging God’s ultimate ownership of their resources. These introspective activities can be powerful tools for reshaping participants’ mindsets and habits around money.

However, one potential drawback of MoneyLife is that its emphasis on biblical principles and spiritual practices may come at the expense of providing highly actionable, practical financial strategies.

Sources indicate that moneyLife is ideal for Christians who are seeking a deeply biblical understanding of money management and are willing to engage in a more studious, reflective learning process. The program is well-suited for those who want to explore the spiritual foundations of financial stewardship and align their money habits with their faith. However, those primarily looking for a simple and easy financial strategy or a more interactive learning experience may find other programs that better fit their needs.

Having gone through all 3 programs, here is my personal experience and recommendations:.

Industry observers note that I can honestly say that True Financial Freedom was a life-changing experience. Bob and Linda’s warm, relatable teaching style made me feel like I was learning from trusted friends who truly cared about my success. The program’s emphasis on creating a personalized financial strategy was a game-changer for me, as it helped me develop a plan that fit my unique situation and goals.

According to recent reports, personally, True Financial Freedom struck that balance better than any of the other programs on the list and gave me the strategy to move forward. My savings, giving, and earning have all increased in significant ways since taking the program.

In a recent development, for those who are drowning in debt and need a clear, structured initiative to get out, I highly recommend Financial Peace University. Dave Ramsey’s no-nonsense approach and the step-by-step “Baby Steps” system can provide the motivation and direction needed to tackle debt head-on. The debt snowball method, in particular, has helped countless people experience quick wins and build momentum on their debt-free journey. Just be prepared for a more intense, boot camp-style learning environment.

If you’re seeking a program that deeply explores the biblical principles behind money management, Crown’s MoneyLife might be the right fit for you. The program’s emphasis on spiritual practices and aligning your finances with your faith can be incredibly powerful for those who want to grow in their understanding of God’s perspective on wealth. However, be prepared for a more academic, reading-intensive learning experience and less focus on highly practical, actionable strategies.

Ultimately, the best program for you will depend on your unique financial situation, learning style, and personal goals. If you’re looking for a grace-filled, practical approach that helps you thrive in God’s Kingdom while making an eternal impact, I highly recommend True Financial Freedom. If you need a structured, intensive blueprint to get out of debt fast, Financial Peace University could be your best bet. And if you desire a deep dive into the biblical foundations of money management, MoneyLife is worth considering.

Regardless of which program you choose, the most vital thing is to take action and invest in your financial education. By doing so, you’ll be better equipped to handle the resources God has entrusted to you and experience the joy and freedom that comes from aligning your finances with your faith.

With a background in marketing for influential organizations such as The Navigators ministry and Highmark Health, he brings a unique perspective to his passion for developing practical discipleship tools. He lives in Greensburg, PA with his wife and two children.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, on-time phone and utility payments rarely reach your credit report, so they don’t help your score. Link the bank account you pay them from to Experian Boost, a free tool that adds them to your Experian report. It’s most worth doing when your credit history is short or your score sits just under a lender’s cutoff.

These bills usually reach a credit report only when one goes unpaid and lands in collections, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau says.

Boost doesn’t wait for the phone tech giant or utility to report. It reads two years of payments in the account you connect and lets you pick which qualifying bills go on your Experian report. Experian shows you right away whether your FICO Score 8, one version of the FICO score, went up.

Only your Experian report gets those payments, so lenders checking your reports at the other two credit bureaus, Equifax and TransUnion, won’t see the gain. Experian also states not every lender uses a score that Boost affects, and most mortgage lenders don’t.

In a recent development, payments by check or through apps like Venmo don’t count. Some rent paid online counts too, though Boost is just one of several ways to get rent reported. You also need enough history for a FICO Score, meaning at least one account active six months or more and one reported in the last six.

Recent findings suggest that take a renter with one credit card who links the account she pays her phone and electric bills from. Boost finds two years of on-time payments on both. Experian says people whose score rose gained 14 points on average. The trade-off is letting Experian see that account’s payment history. Some scores also stay flat or even drop. If hers drops, she can disconnect, and Experian says the score should return to where it was.

Connect your bill-paying account now, ahead of any credit application, and leave it linked so Experian keeps checking for upcoming on-time payments.

Make Each Money Resolution a SMART Goal – Then Automate the First Step

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rewrite each money resolution as a SMART goal, one that’s specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound, so “save more” turns into a dollar amount, a deadline, and a step you take every payday.
  • Neither “save more” nor “get out of debt” says how much, by when, or what to do this week.
  • If you’re paid twice a month and start in January, “save more” becomes “move $250 to a high-yield savings account each payday until it holds $3,000 by June 30.” The account and the amount make it specific, and the balance makes it measurable.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rewrite each money resolution as a SMART goal, one that’s specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound, so “save more” turns into a dollar amount, a deadline, and a step you take every payday. Automate that step, check your progress once a month, and shrink the target instead of quitting if you fall behind.

Neither “save more” nor “get out of debt” says how much, by when, or what to do this week. A resolution without those answers depends on motivation alone, and it stops when your motivation fades.

A SMART goal supplies all three. If you’re paid twice a month and start in January, “save more” becomes “move $250 to a high-yield savings account each payday until it holds $3,000 by June 30.” The account and the amount make it specific, and the balance makes it measurable. It’s achievable as long as $250 a paycheck fits your budget, relevant because $3,000 can pay for a car repair you’d otherwise put on a credit card, and time-bound by June 30.

Industry observers note that the other common money resolutions work the same way. At a 22% interest rate, “get out of debt” becomes “pay off my $2,400 card balance in 12 months by paying $225 a month and charging nothing fresh.” “Spend less on takeout” becomes “keep restaurant and delivery spending to $200 a month, checked every Sunday.”.

According to recent reports, break each target into monthly steps, then automate the first one. Set up a recurring transfer to savings for the day after each payday, or a recurring card payment from checking, so the money moves even in a month you forget about the goal.

Then put a 10-minute check on your calendar for the same day each month to compare your progress with the plan. When a target proves too substantial, lower the amount or move the date instead of dropping the goal. A transfer cut to $150 a paycheck still adds up to at least $1,800 by June 30.

Work on one or two goals at a time, so each gets enough money and attention to make visible progress.

Write your first goal down today with its amount and its date, then schedule its first transfer or payment for the day after your next payday.

#9545. How Unlimited Free Stuff from Amazon Almost Ruined My Retirement

How Unlimited Free Stuff from Amazon Almost Ruined My Retirement

📅 07 Oct 2025 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2033 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It all started last winter when I innocently posted a review for a heated vest I had bought on Amazon.
  • It has been revealed that “Congratulations!
  • I was already aware of Amazon Vine since I had seen product reviews from other people in the program – typically called “Vine Voices.” The basic idea of this program is that you can order stuff from Amazon for free, as long as you agree to review at least 80% of the things you order.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It all started last winter when I innocently posted a review for a heated vest I had bought on Amazon. I was happy with this fun fresh way to beat the winter and wanted to share it with others, so I gave it five stars. But soon after I clicked “Submit”, I got an email from Amazon which stated something like,.

It has been revealed that “Congratulations! You’ve been selected to join Amazon Vine for writing helpful reviews!”.

I was already aware of Amazon Vine since I had seen product reviews from other people in the program – typically called “Vine Voices.” The basic idea of this program is that you can order stuff from Amazon for free, as long as you agree to review at least 80% of the things you order.

“Hey, that’s cool”, I thought, “Who doesn’t like free stuff?

Especially since I’ve already been writing product reviews out of the goodness of my heart – why not be rewarded for it?”.

So without giving it much further thought, I clicked “accept” on their terms and conditions and joined the program.

And so began a saga that has taken me on a surprising journey over the past nine months causing me to:.

Okay, I’ll admit that there were also some upsides. My original idea was partly to save some money, by getting stuff I genuinely would have bought anyway, in a way that sounded fun. And that did happen – I saved at least a few thousand dollars on tools and materials for my construction business and the MMM-HQ Coworking space, for free. Plus, at least some of the motivation for signing up was to put myself through an experiment so I could write this blog article about it. And if you’re reading this, it looks like that happened too.

But I was still surprised at how powerful the combination of small nudges and incentives from Amazon was able to hijack my frugality instincts –  and get me to do a bunch of work that wasn’t really the best use of my time.

Industry observers note that so I figured if we review my journey and break it down with a bit of Behavioral Science, we could all learn a few valuable things by laughing at Mr. Money Mustache’s folly.

Scarcity Brain and the Online Casino Effect.

One of the most interesting books I’ve read in recent years is Michael Easter’s Scarcity Brain. It’s an exploration of the sneaky ways that modern gambling platforms, marketing and social media algorithms are all built upon two weaknesses in our evolutionary programming:.

As I look back now, I realize that I fell straight into those same traps, because the Vine program has all the key properties of a casino or a TikTok feed:.

But occasionally, there will be genuinely useful things like super nice light fixtures, tools and plumbing parts, an EV charger, and even some clothing. My favorite ridiculous Eagle shirt as featured in the Mustachianism music video was an Amazon Vine find.

As were a whole supply of super-realistic artificial plants, which while tacky in principle, have been amazing for hard-to-water courtyard garden areas at the MMM HQ.

I also had a lot of fun roping in friends and coworkers from HQ to help and share in the bounty. I let them help me request and review stuff that they wanted, and then they got to keep it. This seemed like a win/win because we shared the work and the fun of laughing at some of the ridiculous products available.

Still, as I went through this experiment this spring and summer and allowed the system to coax me into doing 80 reviews so I could upgrade my account from Vine Silver to Vine Gold*, I noticed something didn’t feel quite right.

Sources indicate that I was checking the Vine page every day for scores, even when I didn’t actually need anything. It would usually be a bust, but just often enough, something I actually wanted would come up, and I’d order it before it was too late. Scarcity and unpredictable rewards at work.

Recent findings suggest that then the bounty would come, I’d unpack it and photograph it with assembly-line speed so I could batch-write all the reviews once per week or so. For every review I did, I was spending time I’d rather spend doing something else. And for every questionable item I got, I was creating pollution and trash from its manufacturing and packaging – directly contradicting the main values of my life and my reason for writing this blog. And I saw all of this, yet I kept doing it!

So Was This The Downfall of MMM?

According to recent reports, during the worst of this consumerism bender, things were dire. I was getting packages almost every day and my recycling bin was overflowing with cardboard. My son and my girlfriend started laughing at some of my more frivolous purchases, so I found myself discreetly tucking away the boxes when they were around to evade scrutiny.

But eventually, I moved into a recovery stage. I had been letting this habit continue out of laziness and as a form of procrastination: it’s very easy to order shit online and pretend I’m doing something useful, and much more difficult to get moving to do the things that really make my life enjoyable.

But I’m old enough to know that hitting the running trails and the gym for my daily workouts, and making progress on all my construction projects, and focusing on the computer as a creative tool rather than an entertainment device so I can get stuff done like this blog post, are the things that bring me the most joy.

Admittedly, some of the sucky factors of the Vine program helped make it easier to recover too. For every genuinely useful thing I found like a contractor-grade extension cord, I had to scan through endless screens of trinkets which not only wasted my time but actually pissed me off at their very existence.

In a recent development, I also noticed some of the deliberately reviewer-unfriendly features built into the program which reminded me that we reviewers are definitely just low-wage workers rather than any form of VIP. The search functionality is crap, and there is no way to filter or sort the results, because they want you to have to look through everything and they don’t care about the value of your time.

Industry observers note that then there is the hilariously bureaucratic AI-based evaluation system which would occasionally flag my totally tame, factual reviews as “Not meeting our Community Standards” without explaining what the problem was. So I’d have to go in and edit my review, randomly changing a couple of words and maybe some punctuation, and suddenly the AI would be pacified and accept my review. Just dumb.

This is What “Fuck You Money” is For!

It dawned on me that for many people, this is just what “work” looks like. You are given a bunch of tasks and a bunch of rules to follow, in a system you didn’t create and don’t get much say in changing. And then as long as you crank out your TPS Reports without rocking the boat too much, you get your paycheck.

It has been revealed that it reminded me of the Uber Driving experiment I did way back in 2017: as soon as I started working as a driver, I could immediately see dozens of improvements that could be made to the system that would make it function better for both drivers and passengers. But since I wasn’t the boss, nobody wanted to hear my ideas.

Experiences like these remind me that while I love hard work and I love learning fresh things every day, I greatly prefer being the boss. And I’ve gotten pretty damned accustomed to it after 20 years of financial independence, so I see no need to give it up.

One interesting “gotcha” of the Vine program is that they do keep track of all the free stuff you get and send you a 1099 for its retail value at the end of the year. So it’s not really free, just discounted to whatever your marginal tax rate is (about 25% for me this year). If we peek into my account right now, this is how my 2025 is looking:.

So I got about $7000 worth of stuff, and could owe up to $1750 of tax on it. In my case, about 75% of it was “sold” to my business for commercial use (construction supplies which I used on jobs or HQ renovations) so it was effectively converted into real income rather than just tax burden. Some of it was stuff I would have bought anyway for my own house which I’ll gladly pay the taxes on. But there is also probably about $1000 of pure nonsense in there as well, for which I’ll owe a tax bill of $250 as penance for my itchy trigger finger on that “Order” button.

Industry observers note that thanks to some advice from wise readers in the comments (below), I have since learned that in most cases you can mark down this estimated value by 80% before declaring it – because you have effectively eliminated most of the resale value by opening and reviewing the product. Thus my tax bill will be more like $50 rather than $250. More detail in this Reddit discussion here.

So here we are today. While I admit that I didn’t explicitly cancel my account, I used the “Keystone Habit” trick to override the temptation to view the Vine page – mapping that browser bookmark to my daily habits list instead, a little chart which I call my “Badassity Tracker”. The net result is that every time I click it, I’m taken straight to a reminder to get up from the computer and do a quick round of exercise, so I do that instead.

Sources indicate that and of course my writing of this article may be a violation of the terms and conditions of the program (“the first rule of Vine is to not talk about Vine”), so it might even get canceled on me. (and if so I’ll let you know because that would be funny story as well).

But I learned a lot about habits and addiction, and realized that this same feeling might be what drives people into One More Year Syndrome, as they keep working even when they can afford to quit. I have now coached enough people through this situation to see it is way more common than I would have ever guessed.

Sources indicate that as with all MMM articles, there’s a real life lesson in this story. It’s not really about Vine or me or my habits, it’s about you continuing to look at yourself and your life, and always questioning your own assumptions or patterns. And asking the people you trust most for feedback as well:.

Industry observers note that we will never be perfect, but the great news is we don’t have to be. All it takes is a little bit of self reflection and putting ourselves on a slightly better path, as often as we can as life goes on. We are all on a very long journey, so even a tiny course correction can make a huge difference in where we end up.

Real Estate Wholesaling Is a Sales Job, Not an Investment – Check Your State’s Rules

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Real estate wholesaling pays you a fee for putting a home under contract below market and selling the contract to an investor, so it’s a sales job.
  • Sources indicate that the pitch, often from someone selling a course, promises a way into real estate without money or credit.
  • You find them with mailers, lead lists, and calls.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Real estate wholesaling pays you a fee for putting a home under contract below market and selling the contract to an investor, so it’s a sales job. Before you pay for a course, check whether your state requires a license or a disclosure to the seller, and add up what a few months of mailers would cost.

Sources indicate that the pitch, often from someone selling a course, promises a way into real estate without money or credit. What the business takes is a marketing budget and a steady supply of owners who need to sell a rundown house fast.

You find them with mailers, lead lists, and calls. When one agrees, you sign a purchase contract you can sell to another buyer, put down a small good-faith deposit called earnest money, and add an inspection contingency that lets you back out. Then you sell the contract to an investor for an assignment fee, or buy the house and resell it right away in what’s called a double closing.

Either way, you earn a fee for arranging a sale, not a return on property you hold, and it’s the gap between the seller’s price and the investor’s. The Oklahoma Real Estate Commission warns that many sellers don’t realize they’ve agreed to a wholesale deal, or how much the wholesaler makes on it.

Illinois requires a broker’s license once you wholesale twice within any 12 months, and Pennsylvania requires a license for every residential wholesale deal and gives the seller up to 30 days to cancel. Ohio and Connecticut require you and the seller to sign a disclosure before signing the purchase contract, and Oklahoma gives the seller two business days to cancel.

Say a new wholesaler in Illinois spends $3,000 on mailers and lead lists over four months and closes one $8,000 assignment. She clears $5,000 before taxes, and she’d need a broker’s license to sell the second contract she’s working on.

Coaching can cost more than that profit. The Federal Trade Commission alleged that Zurixx used false promises of quick flipping and wholesaling profits to sell $1,997 seminars, then coaching that could run to tens of thousands of dollars. A 2022 settlement permanently banned the organization and its owners from selling coaching.

Before your first mailer goes out, read your state real estate commission’s rules on wholesaling, and tell every seller in writing that you’re a wholesaler, not the final buyer.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that put your first energy-saving dollars into cheap fixes such as weatherstripping, LED bulbs, a programmable thermostat, and low-flow showerheads. They pay for themselves in about one to three years, while new windows can take decades. Check utility and state rebates before you buy anything.

In a recent development, rank each upgrade by its payback, the years its savings take to cover its cost. Cheap fixes rank first because they cost little, even when a major project saves more.

Energy Trust of Oregon, an efficiency nonprofit, puts the payback on cheap fixes at one to three years and on efficient new windows and solar panels at more than 10.

According to recent reports, A 10-window vinyl replacement averaged $22,073 in the 2025 Cost vs. Value report, and Energy Star claims certified windows cut energy bills by up to 13% when they replace single-pane ones. Even on a $3,000 yearly energy bill, a 13% cut is $390 a year, so the job takes more than 55 years to pay back.

Start with a home energy audit from your utility, then work through the cheap fixes:.

Sources indicate that judge bigger projects the same way, using the price after rebates, and only if you’ll own the home longer than the payback. Energy Trust puts attic insulation at four to five years and a high-efficiency furnace, AC, or water heater at six to 10. Energy Star figures a certified heat pump water heater pays back its extra cost in about 2.7 years for a family of four replacing an electric tank. Federal tax credits for efficiency upgrades and solar ended for work done after 2025, but many utilities and some states still pay rebates. Energy Star’s Rebate Finder lists offers by ZIP code.

According to recent reports, A project that adds to your home, rather than replacing something, can raise its assessed value. You can appeal a higher assessment yourself or through Ownwell, which charges only when your tax bill comes down.

Do the sealing and insulating first, since Energy Star claims better insulation may let you choose a smaller, less expensive heat pump.

Latest Update: Budget by Paycheck, Not by the Month – Give Each Bill a Payday

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that if you’re paid weekly or every other week, a monthly budget can balance on paper and still leave you short the week rent is due.
  • In a recent development, say you take home $1,600 every other Friday and your $1,200 rent is due on the 1st.
  • Industry observers note that budgeting by paycheck gives every bill, savings transfer, and spending allowance a specific payday, so each pay period has its own plan and its own leftover.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that if you’re paid weekly or every other week, a monthly budget can balance on paper and still leave you short the week rent is due. Budget by paycheck instead. Put every payday and due date on one calendar, then assign each bill to the check that arrives before it’s due.

In a recent development, say you take home $1,600 every other Friday and your $1,200 rent is due on the 1st. The month’s two checks bring in $3,200, but if the rent comes out of the check that lands just before the 1st, that check has $400 left for two weeks of groceries, gas, and other bills.

Industry observers note that budgeting by paycheck gives every bill, savings transfer, and spending allowance a specific payday, so each pay period has its own plan and its own leftover. In the example, setting aside $600 from each of the two checks before the 1st covers the rent and leaves each check $1,000.

Industry observers note that start with one calendar, on paper or in an app, that holds every payday and due date for the next three months. Include annual and quarterly bills, and divide each by the number of checks left before it’s due. A $720 car insurance bill due 12 checks from now takes $60 from each.

Then spread any bill too big for one check, like the rent, across the checks before it. Give savings transfers a payday too, and split groceries, gas, and fun money evenly across checks. When one check still carries too much, move a due date to the other half of the month. If your pay changes from check to check, start from a budget built on your worst month.

Proposal each month’s bills on two checks, or four if you’re paid weekly. In most years, getting paid every two weeks means 26 checks, so two months bring a third, and weekly pay means 52, so four months bring a fifth. That extra check carries none of the monthly bills, so what it would have set aside for them, like the $600 for rent, is left over. Move it to savings, put it toward debt, or use it to get a month ahead on your bills.

Fill in the calendar before your next payday, and start with your biggest bill, usually rent or the mortgage.

Amelia Earhart Search Find Trees, Not Plane. Mystery Remains

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (429 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A highly anticipated expedition to solve one of aviation’s greatest mysteries has concluded without finding the wreckage of Amelia Earhart’s missing plane.
  • A 17-person team from the Archaeological Legacy Institute and Purdue University recently returned from Nikumaroro, a remote and uninhabited atoll in the Pacific Ocean.
  • Their primary objective was to investigate the Taraia Object, a mysterious shape in a shallow lagoon that researchers first noticed in 2020 on satellite and historical aerial photos.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A highly anticipated expedition to solve one of aviation’s greatest mysteries has concluded without finding the wreckage of Amelia Earhart’s missing plane.

A 17-person team from the Archaeological Legacy Institute and Purdue University recently returned from Nikumaroro, a remote and uninhabited atoll in the Pacific Ocean.

Their primary objective was to investigate the Taraia Object, a mysterious shape in a shallow lagoon that researchers first noticed in 2020 on satellite and historical aerial photos. While some hoped the anomaly was the remnants of Earhart’s Lockheed Electra, the expedition determined it was entirely natural.

In a recent development, the Taraia Object on a satellite image. Located at Nikumaroro. Photo: Archaeological Legacy Institute.

According to recent reports, according to Purdue University officials, the object was a cluster of large fallen trees resting on a sandbar. Much of the debris observed in satellite images had already broken up and washed away, leaving a single Y-shaped piece. The reflective, metallic glint seen from above turned out to be a hardened layer of coral sand coating the wood.

On the way to the atoll. Photo: Purdue Research Foundation.

The five-day operation proved logistically complicated. Workers faced dense brush and a large population of giant coconut crabs. The nocturnal activities of the massive crabs forced the crew to abandon plans to camp on the atoll and to return to the ship each evening. During the day, the crabs simply minded their own business.

One of the crew holds a coconut crab. Photo: Purdue Research Foundation.

Despite the difficulties, researchers recovered a few minor artifacts to study lagoon drift patterns, including a 76cm steel tube.

The team emphasized that ruling out the Taraia Object does not disprove the broader “castaway hypothesis.” For decades, historians have investigated the theory that Earhart and navigator Fred Noonan drifted off course during their 1937 global circumnavigation attempt, landing on Nikumaroro’s reef after failing to find Howland Island.

Sources indicate that amelia Earhart. Photo: amelia.prf.org.

Purdue University, where Earhart once served as a career counselor and aviation advisor, stated that its commitment to the search remains unchanged.

“Amelia Earhart never gave up — she kept pushing boundaries and flying into the unknown,” said Steve Schultz, Purdue’s general counsel and field assistant, after the expedition. “She kept flying, and we will keep searching.”.

For more details, extensive project documentation, and a gallery of expedition photographs, you can visit the official mission site at Amelia.prf.org.

In a recent development, from left to right: Steve Schultz, Sirisha Bandla, and Marc Hagle, members of the research team. Photo: Purdue Research Foundation.

Industry News: Bundling Home & Car Insurance – Compare the Total, Not the Discount

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (489 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, buying your home or renters insurance and your car insurance from one manufacturer usually earns a discount, but the bundle can still cost more than two separate policies.
  • That happens because the discount comes off one company’s own prices.
  • Some companies that sell both home and car insurance take 5% to 15% off your premium for two or more policies, the institute claims.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, buying your home or renters insurance and your car insurance from one manufacturer usually earns a discount, but the bundle can still cost more than two separate policies. Before you switch or renew, get the bundled price and the best separate quotes for the same coverage, and buy whichever total is lower.

That happens because the discount comes off one company’s own prices. The Insurance Information Institute says homeowners insurance for the same house can cost hundreds of dollars more at one insurer than at another.

Some companies that sell both home and car insurance take 5% to 15% off your premium for two or more policies, the institute claims. It also tells buyers to make sure the bundle costs less than buying each policy from a different company.

Say a family asks three insurers to quote the same coverage. The best bundle comes to $3,100 a year, and the cheapest home and car policies from two different companies total $2,850, so buying separately saves $250 a year. Next door, the best bundle costs $600 less than the cheapest separate policies, so the neighbors bundle.

Home, condo, and renters policies usually count toward the discount alongside a car policy. Some insurers also count a life insurance policy or an umbrella policy, which adds liability coverage on top of your home and car policies. Bundling also means one company to call when a storm damages your roof and your car, and some insurers then charge one deductible instead of two. Treat those perks as a tiebreaker when the totals are close.

Separate quotes matter most when your car or your home is hard to insure. A driver with recent speeding tickets may find the lowest car rate at one company and the lowest home rate at another. A home insured through your state’s FAIR plan, the last-resort insurer for homes that private companies won’t cover, can’t be bundled at all, since the plan doesn’t sell car insurance.

Get every quote for the same coverage amounts, deductibles, and add-ons, from an agent or an online comparison tool. A quote with lower coverage amounts can look cheaper only because it pays less after a loss.

Before you split a bundle, ask your current insurer what the policy you’d keep will cost on its own, since dropping the other policy can end its discount.

Compare the best car insurance companies to choose which insurers to ask for quotes.

#9536. Break a Costly Money Habit – Keep the Reward, Swap in a Cheaper Routine

Break a Costly Money Habit – Keep the Reward, Swap in a Cheaper Routine

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (491 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A costly money habit, like ordering delivery after a rough workday, starts with a cue and ends with a reward you want again.
  • Promising to stop leaves the cue and the reward in place.
  • According to recent reports, the reward is often not the thing you buy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A costly money habit, like ordering delivery after a rough workday, starts with a cue and ends with a reward you want again. Work out what sets yours off and what it gives you, then plan a cheaper routine that gives a similar reward, and mark each day you follow it.

Promising to stop leaves the cue and the reward in place. Each time the cue indicates up, you still want the reward, and you have to talk yourself out of it again.

According to recent reports, the reward is often not the thing you buy. Delivery after a rough day gives you a night off from cooking and some comfort. Late-night browsing on shopping sites gives you a distraction, and a lottery ticket gives you a few days of daydreaming about a win.

A cheaper routine can give you that comfort, distraction, or daydream, so you still get what you were after.

Industry observers note that track the habit for a week or two. Each time, note when and where it happens, how you feel, and what you get out of it. The time, place, or mood that keeps coming up is the cue, and the feeling it leaves you with is the reward.

Then set up a swap, a cheaper routine with a similar reward, before the cue comes back. Say two rough workdays a week end in a $30 delivery order, and a frozen dinner costs $7. Keep two in the freezer for those nights and call a friend on the walk home for the comfort. The dinner is plainer than takeout but still spares you the cooking. Those nights now cost about $60 a month instead of $260, a saving of about $200.

In a recent development, take on one habit at a time. Mark each day you choose the swap on a calendar, and move what it saves into savings each week so you can watch the balance grow. A financial therapist can help with a habit that keeps returning despite a good swap.

Industry observers note that give the upcoming routine time. In a University College London study, a new daily habit took 66 days on average to become automatic. Missing a single day had no lasting effect, but about half the volunteers didn’t do it often enough to form the habit. After a slip, run the swap again the next time the cue shows up.

#9535. Freelance Writing Rates – Quote by the Hours a Piece Takes, Not the Word Count

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (493 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Moneycrashers ↗ Open Full Page

Freelance Writing Rates – Quote by the Hours a Piece Takes, Not the Word Count

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (493 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that base every freelance writing quote on all the hours the piece takes, including research, interviews, and revisions.
  • A per-word offer can sound fair and still pay badly, because the word count claims nothing about the hours the piece takes.
  • According to recent reports, say a 1,500-word article takes you 6 hours to research, write, and revise, and you need to earn $75 an hour.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that base every freelance writing quote on all the hours the piece takes, including research, interviews, and revisions. Time a few typical pieces from start to finish, multiply the hours by the hourly rate you need, and quote the total as a project fee. Charge more for specialist topics, rush deadlines, and contracts that buy all rights.

A per-word offer can sound fair and still pay badly, because the word count claims nothing about the hours the piece takes.

According to recent reports, say a 1,500-word article takes you 6 hours to research, write, and revise, and you need to earn $75 an hour. Quote at least $450, which works out to 30 cents a word. A client offering 10 cents a word would pay $150 for the same 6 hours, or $25 an hour.

Thirty cents a word is in line with the Editorial Freelancers Association’s 2026 rate chart, built from a survey of more than 1,100 editorial freelancers. Its median range for work-for-hire articles and essays, which the client owns outright, runs from 25 to 45 cents a word.

Start from the hourly rate you need, which is the yearly income you want plus your business costs and self-employment tax, divided by the hours you can bill clients for. Then time three typical pieces from first research to final revision, including interviews, client calls, and email. Multiply your average hours by that rate, and quote the result as a flat project fee. For a client who pays by the word, divide the fee by the word count to get the per-word rate to ask for.

In a recent development, specialist knowledge, technical or regulated subjects like medicine, credentials such as a CPA license, and rush deadlines all justify a higher fee. In the same rate chart, median ranges for work-for-hire medical and technical writing start at $1 a word. Selling more rights should cost the client more. A contract that buys all rights, or makes the piece work for hire, leaves you nothing to resell or reprint, so price it above one that buys only the right to publish the piece first.

Over time, collect testimonials, quote each latest client above the last, and win more clients directly, since no platform takes a share of what they pay.

Divide every offer by the hours the piece will take, and counter any that fall short of your hourly rate with your project fee.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jost Kobusch is back in Nepal, preparing for the fourth round of his Everest project.
  • “If I am good at something, it’s planning,” the 34-year-old German told ExplorersWeb.
  • According to recent reports, kobusch arrived in Kathmandu two weeks ago, together with friends Nicolas Scheidtweiler, Manuela Brummer, and photographer Alex Pichon.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jost Kobusch is back in Nepal, preparing for the fourth round of his Everest project. His long-term goal is to climb solo in winter, without oxygen, self-supported, and via the Lho La and the West Ridge.

“If I am good at something, it’s planning,” the 34-year-old German told ExplorersWeb. In this case, his plan is to arrive at the mountain in the best shape possible, physically and mentally.

According to recent reports, kobusch arrived in Kathmandu two weeks ago, together with friends Nicolas Scheidtweiler, Manuela Brummer, and photographer Alex Pichon. The group soon moved to Manang in the Annapurna region and began acclimatizing in the Chulu range.

According to recent reports, jost Kobusch (in yellow) scouts around Manang. Photo: Alex Pichon.

Recent findings suggest that the plan was to spend a few nights at altitude and traverse the four Chulu peaks, all above 6,000m. “[However,] expeditions rarely unfold exactly as expected,” Kobusch admitted.

A member in the team felt exhausted after reaching the summit of the second peak, and the group abandoned the traverse there. “At least, we traversed from the summit of Chulu Far East (6,059m) to the top of Chulu East (6,444m) from the southeast,” Kobusch said. He says their line between the two peaks was upcoming.

It has been revealed that the line followed by Kobusch and his team up Chulu East. Photo: Alex Pichon.

Their next plan will be to climb a 7,000m peak in the area before Kobusch moves to the Khumbu in November. “I want to reach 8,000m, but on a different mountain than Everest, before the beginning of winter,” he mentioned.

It has been revealed that he wants to be completely acclimatized by the time he starts working on Everest on December 22, the start of calendar winter. Kobusch will have two photographers in Base Camp, but he will climb alone.

Acclimatization in Manang, Photo: Alex Pichon.

“I need to be able to move efficiently, make good decisions when I’m tired, manage risk alone, and stay comfortable in an environment where very small mistakes can have very serious consequences,” Kobusch recently wrote on social media. He claims that so far, all is going well. “I’m feeling good, I’ve done my homework, and I will start again on Everest better prepared than ever.”.

Kobusch has attempted winter Everest solo on three previous occasions, always via the Lho La and the West Ridge, thus avoiding venturing alone into the Khumbu Icefall.

In his first attempt in 2019-20, he reached the West Shoulder and pushed above 7,300m. On the second attempt in 2021-22, high winds didn’t let him go beyond 6,400m. He planned to try again the following year, but he caught dengue fever while training in Nepal and had to cancel.

In a recent development, once recovered, he soloed Denali in February-March 2023. Everest had to wait one more year, this time due to a back injury. On the third attempt in 2024-25, he reached his highest point yet: 7,537m on December 27.

Kobusch’s highest point is shown with a green circle, and the Hornbein Couloir is the pink line on the 3D map by RealityMaps.

Industry observers note that “The chances of success are not particularly high,” he recently wrote. “If I had to put a number on it, I would say around 20%. But that does not make the attempt meaningless. If anything, it is part of what makes it interesting.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that most billionaires got rich by founding or holding a big stake in a manufacturer that kept growing, not by earning a salary. You can use the same method on a small scale. Own stock through low-cost index funds and hold it for decades, and keep as much ownership as you can in any business you start.

Even a $1 million salary, saved in full, would take 1,000 years to add up to $1 billion.

A stake in a firm is different, because its value rises as long as the company grows and you hold on. Jeff Bezos founded Amazon in 1994 and still owns 8% of it, the largest part of his fortune. Elon Musk’s fortune is mostly the 38% of SpaceX he owns, counting options to buy shares, with less in his nearly 11% of Tesla.

Industry observers note that forbes counts 71% of the 2026 Forbes 400, its list of the richest Americans, as self-made, meaning they built their fortunes rather than inheriting them. The rest started with an inheritance, like Alice Walton, whose fortune comes from her stake in Walmart, the company her father cofounded.

The part you can copy is ownership. If you start a business, keep as much of it as you can, because each share you sell early gives its future gains to the buyer.

Recent findings suggest that don’t copy how much of their wealth they keep in one company, though, since few single stocks pay off like that. Finance professor Hendrik Bessembinder found that four of every seven U.S. stocks since 1926 returned less over their lifetimes than one-month Treasury bills, which are short-term U.S. government debt. The best-performing 4% of companies produced the stock market’s entire net gain over that span.

A broad, low-cost index fund, such as one tracking the whole U.S. stock market, owns thousands of companies, so it holds the few massive winners without you having to pick them. At an assumed 7% average annual return, $10,000 left in one for 30 years grows to about $76,000, because each year’s gain earns returns too. Building wealth on an ordinary income works the same way, by spending less than you earn and investing the gap for decades.

Start investing in stocks with one such fund this month, since in that example the last 10 years add about $37,000, more than the roughly $29,000 the first 20 add.

Pick the broker that will hold that fund from the best online stock brokers for beginners.

Hidesuke Taneishi and Tetsu Hashimoto of Japan are missing on unclimbed Gangapurna West in Nepal’s Annapurna region.

The Japanese pair headed to the 7,140m peak in September, and we heard no further news of them. After a major storm hit Nepal’s mountains three weeks ago, we presumed they had retreated. But now it seems they did not. They have been out of touch since October 15, after encountering severe weather conditions during their attempt to climb the peak, According to News on Nepal.

Industry observers note that hidesuke Taneishi, left, and Tetsu Hashimoto, right, with a support team member in Kathmandu earlier this week. Photo: Cosmo Adventure.

It has been revealed that the Russian team that reached the mountain earlier this month reportedly found no sign of the Japanese climbers on the peak. Bad weather forced the Russians down from their summit attempt at 6,800m.

According to recent reports, A helicopter search-and-rescue operation is now underway, Manang Chief District Officer Mukti Prasad Khanal has confirmed. Today, high-altitude helicopters and drones successfully recovered some of their gear, including trekking poles, near 7,050m, but the climbers themselves remain missing.

Gangapurna West is also known as Asapurna or Peak Lachenal.

#9531. Breaking: My Unexpected Journey to Hormone Replacement (TRT)

📅 16 Dec 2025 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2729 w)

Breaking: My Unexpected Journey to Hormone Replacement (TRT)

📅 16 Dec 2025 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2729 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As a man of Science, I’m supposed to hide my enthusiasm about this somewhat controversial subject, and instead direct you only to the peer-reviewed studies.
  • But man, I feel like I’ve stumbled upon the fountain of youth here.
  • Industry observers note that I’ve been interested in optimization and trying to get the most out of my body and mind since I was a little kid.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As a man of Science, I’m supposed to hide my enthusiasm about this somewhat controversial subject, and instead direct you only to the peer-reviewed studies.

But man, I feel like I’ve stumbled upon the fountain of youth here. And the more I dig into the details and the hype and controversy surrounding the field of Hormone Replacement therapy, the more I need to share the word about it to my fellow middle-aged people (both men and women).

Industry observers note that I’ve been interested in optimization and trying to get the most out of my body and mind since I was a little kid. I started vacuuming up all the training and nutrition books and magazines I could find while I was just a teenager, and that field still remains a favorite of mine over 30 years later. And if you’re a long-time reader here you’ve been reminded plenty of times of this interest, because health has always been the very heart of Mustachianism.

Sources indicate that but a funny thing has been happening in the last ten years: even as I kept honing the healthy living habits and trying my best to improve, there seemed to be a force pulling me back almost as hard. So despite working a bit harder and smarter every year, I still felt myself riding a gradually declining tide of energy, motivation, and physical stamina.

“Perhaps this is just what it means to grow old”, I thought to myself,.

“But I’m still gonna keep fighting it!”.

Sources indicate that yet there was one thing that didn’t quite fit. Why was I having this decline in energy, when some of my older friends weren’t? And why was I still seeing people out there in their 50s, 60s and well beyond doing things that I felt too tired to do today?

One of these tireless friends is a guy named Kevin, who is the personification of the highly energetic successful middle-aged man. He’s a semi-retired serial entrepreneur (and extreme rock climber) who lives in Boulder. And through an interesting twist of fate, in April of 2025 he invited me out for a hike right around the time I was doing all this wondering. And during this hike (and climb) he told me about his latest venture, a boutique men’s health company that specializes in helping men just like us get their youth back through the process of testosterone replacement therapy.

In a recent development, long story short: his ideas planted a seed in my head, which led to a bunch of research and a growing interest in trying TRT myself. I had of course heard about the process, but for some reason never considered doing it until I heard Kevin’s enthusiasm: he had been on it for several years, and according to him it is a “night and day difference” in all the things you want in life: energy, focus, thinking speed, and of course physical health.

In a recent development, another convenient twist of fate is that I happen to be dating an REI doctor – a Reproductive Endocrinologist and Infertility specialist who has two board certifications in exactly the relevant bodily systems that are affected by these hormones. And while she was initially skeptical that I needed more Testosterone (and in her practice she regularly sees the downsides of men taking the stuff too early in life and thus compromising their own fertility), she has followed along and helped me learn at each step of this process, eventually becoming fully in support of the program.

So I signed up as a test customer for Kevin’s latest company, which is called Bolt Health. I worked with their doctor to get a baseline blood test and review my numbers compared to all the past tests I’ve collected, and as it turned out, my levels had been dropping consistently over the years, and the latest test was by far the lowest ever.

Even more telling, my age-related drop in Testosterone was correlating perfectly with my decline in energy and motivation:.

Recent findings suggest that the next step was a prescription for a tiny daily dose of supplemental T, which arrived at my house the next week along with instructions for how to use it. And so began the journey.

Now let’s jump forward seven months to the present day as I write this.

Industry observers note that and wow, what a great year it has been! I only wish I had known and tried this a few years earlier, because I’m getting a lot more out of my life.

It’s not a night-and-day difference for me, but more like a 50% boost in overall youthfulness and energy. The biggest subjective change is that I just don’t have sucky tired days anymore, which was the main problem with my life before: wasting too much of my precious freedom due to not having the energy to enjoy it.

Sources indicate that this is why I’ve become somewhat of an evangelist for hormone replacement therapy for people from about age 45 onwards. It won’t work for everyone – if your levels are already pretty high, you don’t get the same boost. Two of my male friends tried TRT and quit because they didn’t notice any benefit. But these same two guys already had plenty of energy to begin with, which is usually a sign that the body has what it needs.

It turns out I am very late to this party. Although Testosterone supplementation started out as a niche practice in the 1940s, from the 2010s onward it has been everywhere.

TRT is the reason you see every actor suddenly showing up buff overnight for their superhero roles and it’s also why so many of today’s CEOs don’t look anything like yesterday’s CEOs.

In many cases, it has gone too far with young men using it just to gain muscle for the beach or the football field, and questionable online providers (aka “Prescription Mills”) handing out prescriptions to anyone with a valid credit card – with profit as their sole motive. It became overhyped in certain pockets of Bro Culture, where every Bro eventually receives the advice “Bro! You need to get on the T!” from another Bro, and therefore does it. And some of this reputation surely contributed to my own skepticism.

In a recent development, but there’s a lot of valid science behind TRT, if you’re the right candidate and you take the right dosage. And because of that, I feel it is probably under-hyped in my own demographic, the Nerdy Tech Worker Semi Retired Dad contingent. And that’s why I’m writing this blog post, because there are a lot of us out there.

Many of us just tend to work with what we were given, and accept that aging means slowing down. And for those of us already enjoying an early retirement, we have the option of unlimited rest and recuperation time, so who really cares if we get tired a bit more often? After all, what better way to flex one’s wealth than with a decadent Tuesday Afternoon Nap while everyone else is stuck in the office?

Recent findings suggest that while this seemingly healthy attitude has a lot of positive aspects, it can also mask a real problem which may be easily fixable. Because sometimes, the only thing that’s even better than an afternoon nap, is having the energy and motivation to go out for an afternoon hike, bike ride or adventure with friends. More energy is also pretty darned useful if you’re still raising kids or trying to do well in your career as a person over 45.

How it Actually Works (and What Happened to Me).

Distilling all of the fluffy discussion above into the simplest possible answer: TRT means using a tiny needle to inject a few drops of clear liquid just below the surface of your skin. And you do this by yourself at home, ideally once every morning.

Here’s one of the baby needles I use for my daily dose.The typical serving is less than one tenth of a milliliter, which is only a few drops.

In a recent development, and while the term “needle” sounds scary to some, this is very different from the monstrosities they use to draw blood from your veins. This one is so miniature that you don’t need special training to use it, and you usually don’t even feel it.

So I began doing this to myself on May 1st of this year, while keeping a daily journal of my results along the way. The results seemed to be almost immediate in all the promised areas, but I know how powerful the Placebo Effect can be so I kept my skeptic’s hat on to see what would happen in the long run.

I was seeing increased energy and motivation as well as lean weight gain through the whole spring and summer, but I remember the first truly shocking observation happened during a mountain vacation in July. I was part of a multi-family trip with lively adults, chaotic kids, early mornings, late nights with a few drinks, very intense high altitude sunshine and nonstop physical activities. It was just the type of situation that would drain my energy pretty quickly in the past.

Sources indicate that but on day three I went out on a solo mountain bike ride to explore the area, and as I was climbing a long ascent with the blazing sun cooking me from every angle I just somehow kept having plenty of energy to keep climbing. Then I came down and joined the group for a few games of full-sun pickleball, biked back up the mountain to our cabin, and the story of unlimited energy went on from there.

“Hot Damn”, I thought to myself, “I don’t know whose youthful and tireless body I have inherited here but I’d sure like to keep it!”.

In August, the Bolt Health program scheduled a follow-up blood test for me and sure enough, my Testosterone levels had been boosted from 415 to 730ng/dL, bringing me from the low side of normal to the higher side.

Industry observers note that many labs define “normal” as anywhere between 300 and 1000, which seems strange to me given the huge effect this hormone has on your wellbeing. It’s a bit like saying “Most cars have between 90 and 300 horsepower, so it doesn’t really matter what engine you have”.

I mean yeah, either one will still get you down the road, but which one would you rather be driving?

Since then, it has just been more of the same good results. My improvements ramped up and then just stayed there – so I’m operating at a new, much higher and more enjoyable level of functioning. Energy and motivation are no longer a problem, and I even find myself willing to make longer-term aims again (before this everything beyond same-day planning felt overwhelming). And my body seems to just want to gain strength and size with any excuse. Heavy weights feel lighter and the hard manual labor I still like to spend my time on feels easier for longer. It’s nice to be young again!

So Why Doesn’t Everyone Do This?

Recent findings suggest that when you dig into the details, hormone replacement is mired in a soup of both real and incorrect information about both its benefits and its risks. And then our well-meaning medical establishment locks this whole container of soup deep in the cabinet with a label that says, “Needs Further Study”. But if you summarize the findings on both sides of the issue, you’ll see this:.

Stuff you should do BEFORE trying TRT:.

The modern American Lifestyle is a Testosterone and Health Crusher. It’s a miracle that anybody feels good ever with the crap that people do to their bodies. So if you’re not already doing all the simple, natural, outdoor things that naturally boost your health, energy, and hormone levels, you’ll want to start with these first. You can find a pretty complete list on my oft-cited Badassity Tracker page.

Since I was already doing all of these things pretty consistently, I felt ready to take the next step and at least consider hormone supplementation. But wait, there’s more!

Many of the problems above are more likely to appear when the body is flooded with too much testosterone. In the bad old days, TRT was administered by sticking a pellet beneath your skin or injecting a large amount into the butt which then gets used up over the next several weeks. One friend recounted a story of extreme moodiness when the pellet was first implanted, ramping down to tiredness by the time the hormone was all gone.

More modern providers like Bolt have fixed this problem by breaking the dose into much smaller servings which you administer each day. The idea is that your levels remain stable, and you need a lot less overall which reduces side effects.

For my part, I have not had any of the negative side effects because I was a pretty ideal candidate in the first place: 50 years old with depressed Testosterone levels but an otherwise healthy lifestyle and no risk factors.

According to recent reports, my hope in sharing this article is to be transparent and hopefully take some of the stigma out of this subject of other people who might benefit. Because in our modern over-connected world, everybody has an opinion on your life, even when you didn’t ask them.

Sources indicate that and it’s not just men – many women in this same age group benefit from Estrogen replacement (and there are even interesting stories about female testosterone supplementation in certain situations as this author shares). The point is that aging is normal, but in some cases there’s a pretty easy way to make it slower.

It has been revealed that the great news is that Testosterone itself is a cheap and widely available substance, typically under $50 per month even for people like me without conventional insurance or drug coverage. The expensive part (here in the US) is just the doctor stuff – consultations, blood tests, ongoing analysis and prescription renewals and so on.

The company that I used is positioned as a premium provider, bundling these services along with a bunch of other men’s health perks and deliveries for a few hundred dollars, which is expensive relative to most other parts of my budget, but still cheap if I consider the life and financial benefits of being 20-50% more energetic and productive.

If you want to be on this program, your final decision will hinge on your income, insurance coverage if applicable, whether your existing doctor can already help you, and how much service and advice you’re willing to pay for.

Note: I decided not to become a Bolt health affiliate because I wanted to write this article without conflict of interest. And I can honestly say, Bolt’s product and service seem great to me because I know and trust the people who run it. But  it’s also the only one I’ve tried. So I don’t know much about the competition and there may be other good options out there. At the very minimum, you can always try one service and switch to another if you don’t like the first one.

It has been revealed that I’ve got lots more to say on money and early retirement, and lots of interesting projects in the works now too. So I’m thankful to have stumbled upon this booster for all aspects of life, so I can do more of everything else, for even more decades than I had expected.

I wish this same type of good fortune for you, however you create it.

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Paying off a non-medical collection helps only newer credit scores.
  • Sources indicate that on its own, paying won’t take a collection off your reports.
  • Recent findings suggest that FICO claims its Score 9 and Score 10 ignore a collection agency’s account once it’s reported paid in full or settled to a zero balance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Paying off a non-medical collection helps only newer credit scores. FICO Score 9 and 10 and VantageScore 3.0 and 4.0 stop counting a collection once it’s paid, while paying does nothing for FICO Score 8 and older versions. Before you pay anything, get the collector’s terms in writing, including whether it will delete the account from your credit reports.

Sources indicate that on its own, paying won’t take a collection off your reports. It stays seven years from the missed payment that started it, paid or not, unless it’s a medical collection, which the credit bureaus drop once it’s paid.

Recent findings suggest that FICO claims its Score 9 and Score 10 ignore a collection agency’s account once it’s reported paid in full or settled to a zero balance. VantageScore’s models have ignored paid collections since version 3.0 in 2013. Paying does nothing for FICO Score 8 or older versions.

Recent findings suggest that that difference matters for a mortgage. The Federal Housing Finance Agency lets lenders selling loans to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac choose Classic FICO, an older model that still counts a paid collection, or VantageScore 4.0, which ignores it. Ask your lender which one it uses, and whether the loan requires collections paid off by closing.

Handle the collector in this order.

According to recent reports, say a collector agrees in writing to settle your $900 cable bill for $500. FICO Score 9 then treats the zero-balance account as paid and stops counting it, but the report lists it as settled, not paid in full. The $400 forgiven counts as taxable income unless an exception such as insolvency applies, with or without a Form 1099-C reporting it.

Pull your free weekly reports at AnnualCreditReport.com after you pay, and dispute the account with any bureau whose report doesn’t match the signed letter, sending a copy as proof.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The three-man Russian team returned to Everest’s West Ridge but found the route even more difficult than they expected. After two days of struggle, they’re heading back to Base Camp.

In a recent development, on October 20, Andrei Vasiliev, Serguey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov went back up to the Lho La and pitched their tent on the wide plateau beyond. They still had time to fix more rope higher up.

“We moved…over terrain we’d already covered on the previous rotation,” the climbers texted to team member Natalya Belyankina, who had to abandon the expedition due to illness.

“The weather is good: sunny, with light winds, but cold,” they noted. “Progress was painfully slow today due to heavy packs and a persistent cough,” the climbers noted later.

In a recent development, on Wednesday, they hoped to reach 7,500m, spend the night there, check the route ahead, and then retreat to the plateau. However, they didn’t get as far as they had planned.

“We didn’t cover much ground today,” leader Andrei Vsiliev texted Anna Piunova of The Mountain Club. “The route is no walk in the park. We have to climb steep snowy slopes that conceal rock sections underneath.”.

According to recent reports, to make things worse, they found no suitable bivy spots at their highest point, so they had to retreat to a place where they could pitch their tent for the night. Today, they were just too exhausted to keep going.

“We’re heading down; we’re sick and need to recover,” Vasiliev told Belyankina. “We can barely keep moving.”.
